science.title: 1st-ever detection of a dying star's 'final nuclear heartbeat' challenges what we know about our sun's eventual death
science.description: null As ubiquitous as the sun is to us today, our star is not eternal; one day, albeit in billions of years, it will die. While massive stars die in supernova explosions, the sun and stars of similar mass die quieter deaths. But that doesn't mean these stars completely go out with a whimper. New observations collected using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), the world's largest radio telescope comprised of 66 antennas in northern Chile, reveal that the sun's death throes may be different from what scientists had initially believed. NASA Jet Propulsion Lab (JPL) researcher Raghvendra Sahai, who led the investigation, explained the shape the ALMA observations took: "It's essentially a physical snapshot of an event that, until now, we've mostly inferred from theoretical models. We've caught, for the first time, a star's final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas." Sun-like stars "die" when they run out of hydrogen in their cores. This means that the fusion of hydrogen to helium ceases in the stellar core, and because this nuclear process is a star's main energy source, the star no longer has the outward push to support itself against the inward push of its own gravity. As the star's core collapses to create a stellar remnant called a white dwarf , the outer layers where hydrogen is still fusing to form helium swell out. This expansion leads to a relatively short-lived " red giant " phase. Eventually, these outer layers will cool and disperse, leaving the central white dwarf surrounded by a so-called "planetary nebula" shell of debris. During the red giant phase, as the stellar core is surrounded by shells of hydrogen and helium, these layers are occasionally rocked by flares in nuclear activity called thermal pulses. During these episodes, stellar material is flung into space. To better understand this phase in stellar evolution, the team focused ALMA on a star called IRAS 06530-0213, located around 12,000 light-years away in the constellation Monoceros. This revealed a giant ring of gas that appears to be a frozen fossil of the star's last thermonuclear flare-up. This thermonuclear fossil rings an hourglass-shaped planetary nebula in the act of forming. "Most of us think of stars as unchanging points of light, but this is a real-time snapshot of a star's death throes," Sahai said. "It's the brief, violent transition between a bloated red giant and a glowing planetary nebula, frozen mid-action." It represents the first direct evidence of the last thermal pulse before this kind of star enters the final phase of its life. science.title: Double asteroid solar eclipse caught on camera | Space photo of the day for Nov. 24, 2026
science.description: null (Image credit: ESA) A spacecraft far from Earth beamed home a rare sight: a solar eclipse caused by one asteroid casting its shadow on another. What is it? The image shows the Didymos double asteroid system , which consists of the larger Didymos and its moonlet, Dimorphos. In this image, Dimorphos' shadow can be seen on the surface of Didymos. The image was captured by the European Space Agency's (ESA's) Hera probe, which was sent to rendezvous with Didymos. Once there, Hera's job is to inspect the system to study the aftermath of NASA's historic DART mission (Double Asteroid Redirect Test), which slammed a kinetic impactor into Dimorphos in September 2022 in an attempt to alter its orbit and thus the trajectory of the entire two-asteroid system. Such missions, should they ever be needed in the future, could potentially redirect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. Why is it incredible? For one, this image is incredible given that it was beamed home by Hera while it approaches Didymos some 121 million miles (195 million kilometers) away from Earth. But more than that, this image reveals incredible details of the Didymos system. Scientists call Didymos a "rubble pile" asteroid , meaning it's a loose body made up of boulders, dust, gravel and other bits of the solar system held together by the asteroid's own gravity. In the image, many of these irregular boulders and rocks can be seen strewn across Didymos and its moonlet. Hera will reach the system on Nov. 25, and ESA will release the first full images from the mission.

science.title: China launching 1st international astronaut to Tiangong space station today: Watch it live
science.description: null China will send an international astronaut to its Tiangong space station today (Nov. 24) for the first time ever, and you can watch the landmark liftoff live. A Long March 2F rocket is scheduled to launch the Shenzhou-24 mission from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China today at 7:18 p.m. EST (0018 GMT and 8:18 a.m. Beijing time on Nov. 25). You can watch the liftoff live here at Space.com, courtesy of China Central Television (CCTV). China rolls out the Long March 2F rocket for its Shenzhou-24 astronaut mission on Nov. 17, 2026. (Image credit: CCTV) Shenzhou-24 will be China's 18th crewed spaceflight to date and its 12th astronaut mission to Tiangong , a three-module station that the nation finished assembling in low Earth orbit in late 2022. Those numbers may sound rather prosaic. But today's flight will make history, marking the first time that China has ever launched a foreign national to space. That trailblazer is Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a former pilot in Pakistan's armed forces who will be the first person from his country ever to reach orbit. (Adventurer Namira Salim is the first Pakistani ever to fly to the final frontier, doing so on a Virgin Galactic suborbital mission in October 2023 .) China and Pakistan began paving Ali's path to Tiangong in February 2025 , with the signing of a spaceflight cooperation agreement in Islamabad. Pakistan then selected two astronaut candidates, who traveled to China for training. We didn't learn which Pakistani astronaut was picked for Shenzhou-24 until Monday night (Nov. 23), when China announced the mission's crew. This is not out of the ordinary, by the way; China generally doesn't reveal the identity of Shenzhou astronauts until the day before launch. This is in keeping with the nation's broader spaceflight ethos, which prizes keeping things close to the vest. Ali is flying as a payload specialist. The other Shenzhou-24 astronauts are commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer ​Wu Yi. Tang also flew on the Shenzhou-12 and Shenzhou-17 missions, which launched in June 2021 and October 2023, respectively. He will be the first person to visit Tiangong three times, according to the state-run Xinhua news agency. Shenzhou-24 will be the first spaceflight for Wu. Tang and Wu are expected to live aboard Tiangong for six months, the usual Shenzhou rotation. But Ali will stay in orbit for just a week or so, coming back down to Earth with Zhang Zhiyuan and Lai Ka-ying of the Shenzhou-23 mission, which launched on May 24 . According to the South China Morning Post, the third Shenzhou-23 crewmate, Zhu Yangzhu, will stay behind when Ali leaves, living aboard Tiangong until Shenzhou-24 comes home. Zhu will therefore become the first Chinese astronaut ever to spend a year in orbit, a milestone that will allow China to prep for long-duration missions to the moon and other deep-space locales.

science.title: Russia launches Progress 97 cargo ship to the International Space Station (video)
science.description: null Russia's latest freighter is on its way to the International Space Station. The robotic Progress 97 cargo craft launched atop a Soyuz rocket from the Russia-run Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan today (Nov. 24) at 5:17 a.m. EST (1013 GMT; 3:17 p.m. Baikonur time), carrying several tons of supplies for the astronauts aboard the orbiting lab. If all goes to plan, Progress 97 will arrive at the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday (Nov. 26), docking with its Poisk module. But the freighter won't stay at that particular locale for long. A Russian Soyuz rocket launches the uncrewed Progress 97 cargo ship to the International Space Station from Baikonur Cosmodrome, Kazakhstan on Nov. 24, 2026. (Image credit: NASA) The cosmonauts currently living on the ISS — Pyotr Dubrov, Anna Kikina and Sergey Teteryatnikov — will unload Progress 97 through Poisk. But the freighter will then hop over to a different port, according to journalist and space historian Anatoly Zak: the aft one of the PrK transfer tunnel, which leads to Russia's Zvezda service module. The PrK port is the best site for engine burns that boost the orbit of the ISS, a service that Progress freighters regularly provide. But Progress 97 cannot unload its cargo through that port because the PrK transfer tunnel has been sealed off, due to an ongoing air leak that was first documented in 2019. Progress-97 is therefore "the first cargo mission scheduled to unload its cargo and perform orbit corrections of the ISS at different docking ports," Zak wrote on the site he runs, RussianSpaceWeb.com. Progress 96 cargo spacecraft packed with science and supplies approaches the International Space Station for a docking on Sept. 19, 2026. (Image credit: NASA) The Progress 97 mission, which Russia calls Progress MS-36, was originally expected to launch this past August, according to Zak. But the liftoff was pushed back several times, most significantly by the collapse of the service platform at Baikonur's Site 31 in November 2025. It took Russia about three months to repair the platform, leading to a series of delays. Progress 97 will likely stay docked to the ISS for about six months, after which it will be loaded up with trash and sent home to burn up in Earth's atmosphere . Japan's HTV-X vehicle and Northrop Grumman's Cygnus spacecraft are similarly expendable. The only currently operational ISS cargo craft that's reusable is SpaceX's Dragon capsule, which makes parachute-aided ocean splashdowns at the end of its missions.

science.title: Severe eczema healed by novel immune-calming pill in clinical trial
science.description: Eczema causes itchy, inflamed rashes on the skin Evgeniia Gordeeva/Getty Images Over a third of people with moderate to severe eczema taking part in a clinical trial have seen their skin completely or almost completely clear up after taking an experimental pill for four months. The drug targets a part of the immune system that causes eczema when it gets stuck in overdrive, and it may be preferable to the current standard treatment, which has to be injected. “It definitely looks promising,” says Gayle Ross at the Royal Melbourne Hospital. Read more Chronic inflammation messes with your mind. Here’s how to calm it Eczema, or atopic dermatitis, is a chronic skin condition characterised by itchy, inflamed rashes and broken skin that can become infected. It is driven by an overactive immune pathway involving two signalling proteins called interleukin-4 and interleukin-13. Advertisement In 2017, the companies Sanofi and Regeneron received approval in the US for their jointly developed eczema drug dupilumab, which blocks interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 signalling. But, although the medication is effective , it has had limited uptake in the US because it must be injected under the skin and costs up to $59,000 per year for those without insurance coverage. Now, another company, Kymera Therapeutics, has developed an alternative treatment that can be taken in pill form, called KT-621. It targets the same immune pathway as dupilumab but degrades a protein called STAT6 that is activated downstream from interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 in the development of eczema. Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter In the clinical trial , 244 adults with an average age of 39 and moderate to severe eczema were randomised to take KT-621 at three different doses or a placebo pill every day for 16 weeks. Those taking the most effective dose experienced an average 72 per cent reduction in their eczema severity on a standard scale, compared to 27 per cent in the placebo group. What’s more, 38 per cent of participants taking KT-621 had completely healed skin or almost completely healed skin by the end of the trial. “These results exceeded our expectations,” said Terence Rooney , the chief medical officer of Kymera Therapeutics, when announcing the results in a webcast on 23 November. He showed before-and-after photos of one man who had had severe eczema all over his torso at the beginning of the trial, which disappeared by the end. “It’s obviously early days and the trial had relatively small patient numbers, but [KT-621] looks like it has similar efficacy to dupilumab, which is currently the standard of care for moderate to severe atopic dermatitis, and it would be nice to have an oral option as opposed to an injection,” says Ross. Here's what you need to know. November's full moon occurs at 9:53 a.m. EST (1453 GMT) on Nov. 24, as the lunar disk passes opposite the sun in our sky, making it appear fully lit from our perspective. The November full moon is often referred to as the Beaver Moon because it rises around the time the small mammals are hard at work building their lodges in preparation for the winter. Viewers in the U.S. can even get a detailed look at the full moon ahead of local moonrise thanks to a free supermoon livestream from the Virtual Telescope Project (VTP), starting at 10:30 a.m. EST (1530 GMT) today. The Beaver Moon is also set to be a dazzling supermoon , because it turns full as the natural satellite passes within 90% of perigee , when it is at its closest to Earth in its 27-day elliptical orbit. When to see the Beaver Moon November's full moon will be below the horizon for stargazers in the U.S. at the moment it turns full. Signs of unrest began in late October 2026. On October 27, seismic sensors recorded a sharp uptick in activity, and Japan’s Meteorological Agency reported that the first photographs of the eruption were captured. Soon after, sensors on several satellites began to capture an array of observations. The OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 captured the left image on October 26, when the coast was still quiet. On November 11, Landsat 9 got its first clear view of the land the submarine volcano has built (right). A shortwave-infrared signature, a sign of the eruption’s heat, is shown in orange. A faint gray volcanic plume drifts southeast of the vent, and a streak of floating pumice stretches across the water in the same direction. A false-color backscatter radar image from the NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) satellite offered an even earlier look at the eruption. The eruption appears to have added roughly 50 hectares (125 acres) of new beach, about the area of 90 American football fields. That would enlarge the island by about 1.7 percent. The new land adjoins the southeast beach where American troops landed on February 19, 1945, beginning one of the bloodiest battles in the history of the U.S. Marines. The location of the eruption is no surprise to scientists. In addition to the 2023 eruption off the southeast coast, Iwo Jima had an eruption off its west coast in August 2025, said Daniel Slayback, a scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. science.title: Will astronauts farm on the moon? Scientists successfully grow potatoes in simulated lunar dust
science.description:
Julian Dossett is a freelance writer living in Santa Fe, New Mexico. He primarily covers the rocket industry and space exploration and, in addition to science writing, contributes travel stories to New Mexico Magazine. In 2022 and 2024, his travel writing earned IRMA Awards. Previously, he worked as a staff writer at CNET. He graduated from Texas State University in San Marcos in 2011 with a B.A. in philosophy. He owns a large collection of sci-fi pulp magazines from the 1960s.

It's no secret that NASA is working towards a permanent presence on the moon. The space agency even plans to build a moon base for its astronauts to call home. But humans living inside lunar habitats around the clock will need three square meals a day, so researchers have been working on how to grow food on the moon. To that end, a team from the College of Agricultural Sciences at Oregon State University have been raising potatoes in simulated moon dust with promising results. The researchers published their findings Nov. 20 in the Microgravity science journal. "We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter," Aymeric Goyer, associate professor at OSU's Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, said in a statement . "That's an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the moon." To grow the spuds, the scientists used five different materials that are similar to regolith , the dust and rocks that cover the moon's surface. The moon contains various regions with unique surface makeups, so the materials they used simulated regolith from both lunar mare and lunar highland regions. The secret ingredient was vermicompost, a soil that's rich in nutrients. The team added different levels of vermicompost to the simulated regolith to grow the potatoes. They figured out that fake regolith mixed with 30 percent vermicompost worked about as well as growing potatoes with regular soil. Oregon State University researchers David Handy and Aymeric Goyer studying potatoes grown in lunar regolith. (Image credit: Aymeric Goyer/David Handy/OSU) "We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith by reducing plant exposure to harmful compounds," David Handy, a postdoctoral researcher in Goyer's lab, said in the same statement. The idea is that astronauts in the future could bring a little nutrient-rich soil with them and mix it with regolith to grow potatoes. After all, it'd cost a ton to ship all that food from Earth. NASA funding supported this research.

Microwave sounders provide critical measurements of temperature and moisture in the atmosphere, which significantly influence weather patterns. The SMBA instruments could improve the medium-range forecasts for NOAA’s National Weather Service. The NEON mission is a collaboration between NASA and NOAA. The mission is led by NOAA, which provides funding, technical requirements, and postlaunch operations. NASA will manage the development of the NEON satellites and launch them for NOAA. Alan is also a novelist—his debut novel, the urban fantasy The Sixth Borough, is available now.

Sports in space have a long and proud tradition, whether it's Alan Shepard playing golf on the moon or the crew of the ISS hosting their own version of the Summer Olympics . The future looks bright as well, with the foundation of the Space Games Federation , the self-described "first governing and sanctioning body for competitive sports played in zero or micro-gravity," co-founded by a NASA astronaut. Not to be outdone, science fiction has expanded the idea of zero-g and low-gravity sports to their logical extent, imagining everything from Doctor Who's zero-g squash to the advanced, gamified combat simulations of Ender's Game. There was even Space Jam 's alien basketball game for the fate of the planet, though the gravity-defying antics there come from cartoon shenanigans rather than a zero-g playing field. As humanity edges closer to colonizing our neighbors through projects like the Artemis Program and its ambition to establish habitats on the moon, our imaginations have to expand to encompass not only how we'll live in space but also how we'll play. The rules change when gravity disappears (Image credit: Zero-G) We rarely think about it in an Earth context, but every sport is heavily influenced by gravity. It defines how balls arc, how quickly players can move, and even how we orient ourselves in play spaces. Remove the gravity, and all of those assumptions and mechanics evaporate as well. "First of all, in zero g, Isaac Newton will win every time," Les Johnson, former Chief Technologist for NASA, told Space. Les is a physicist with over 35 years of experience working at Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, as well as a science fiction author. "'For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction,'" quotes Johnson. "This is very difficult to simulate in real life due to gravity; special effects often try to compensate. With today’s AI and green screens, it can actually look good on screen." In a microgravity scenario, the concept of up and down is no longer relevant. Suddenly, the playing field expands from a single, fixed plane to a fully three-dimensional space that includes height. (Image credit: Netflix) Momentum is also a completely different beast. Instead of being able to quickly stop and pivot the way you can during terrestrial sports, once you start moving in microgravity, you keep going until something stops you. science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 23, 2015: Blue Origin sticks 1st-ever rocket landing from space with its suborbital New Shepard rocket
science.description: null On Nov. 23, 2015, a Blue Origin rocket made a historic landing. Before this time, all rockets were single-use only — even SpaceX's rockets. Blue Origin changed the concept forever. After launching the New Shepard capsule safely into space, the rocket started heading back to Earth. It flew towards a landing pad, reignited its engine to slow down and touched down softly on the ground . This was the first successful vertical landing from space in history. The Blue Origin milestone meant that rockets could be reused for multiple missions, which saves money and reduces waste. (Image credit: Blue Origin) Why it mattered Today, SpaceX may be the most well-known for landing its Falcon 9 rocket boosters from orbit. The company's triple-core Falcon Heavy boosters can also land vertically and its massive Starship megarocket can even return to the launch site to be caught by giant metal arms. But in the end, Blue Origin did it first. Blue Origin's New Shepard booster landing kicked off an era of vertical launch and vertical landings for rockets that continues to this day. It may have even outlasted the New Shepard rocket. Since that first landing, Blue Origin has launched 17 suborbital astronaut flights with New Shepard, and 21 more uncrewed flights for a total of 38 missions between April 2015 and 2026. The company reused its New Shepard boosters repeatedly (though it did lose one during an uncrewed launch after a technical issue.) But in January 2026, the company announced a pause in New Shepard flights for two years so that it could focus on moon lander projects. But Blue Origin did not abandon rocket landings. Indeed, the company's success with New Shepard led it to build vertical landing into its larger orbital rocket, New Glenn, which made its first successful landing 2025 — nearly 10 years after that first touchdown. Blue Origin has since reflown a New Glenn booster , and is developing a new rocket engine called Northstar for even better performance. Want more space history? science.title: Weird 'potato chips' and 'ghostly rocks' on Mars spotted by NASA rovers Curiosity and Perseverance
science.description: null NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers have spotted a bizarre assortment of Martian oddities, from potato chip-like rocks and ghostly white formations to mysterious patterns etched into the Red Planet's surface. While their appearances may be unusual, these formations offer scientists something far more valuable than a collection of curious snapshots: clues to the geological processes that shaped Mars over billions of years. In particular, the rocks and mineral deposits could help researchers piece together the planet's watery past and identify environments that may once have been capable of supporting microbial life. NASA's Curiosity rover recently wrapped up a drilling campaign at a location nicknamed "Nazca," where scientists have been examining unusual disk-shaped crystal formations embedded in the surrounding bedrock. Some of the features are so thin and flat that the mission team likened them to potato chips, according to a statement from the space agency. NASA's Curiosity rover captured a close-up view of unusual, disk-shaped crystal formations embedded in Martian bedrock using its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI) on Nov. 7, 2026 (Sol 5067). The thin, flattened formations resemble tiny potato chips. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS) Curiosity used its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI), mounted on the end of its robotic arm, to capture detailed close-up images of the formations on Nov. 7 — the rover's 5,067th Martian day , or Sol 5067. The rover also used its ChemCam instrument to study the rocks' chemical composition, while samples from the Nazca drill site were delivered to its onboard Sample Analysis at Mars (SAM) instrument for further analysis. Meanwhile, NASA's Perseverance rover has been investigating a collection of unusually bright rocks in an area called "Idubi," located in the “Lac de Charmes” region outside Jezero Crater. The rover captured images of the formations on Oct. 29, 2026 (Sol 2023), revealing pale, ghostly-looking rocks that stand out dramatically against the darker, dust-covered Martian landscape. Data from Perseverance's SuperCam instrument revealed that the rocks are rich in hydrated silica rather than being typical igneous rocks. That discovery has scientists particularly interested. On Earth, hydrated silica can form in environments involving hydrothermal activity or groundwater. These deposits are also capable of preserving microscopic fossils, making them valuable targets in the search for evidence of ancient life, according to another statement from NASA.
